newsitem.title: USA: Pollution in U.S. rivers becoming harder to fight.
newsitem.headline: Pollution in U.S. rivers becoming harder to fight.

text.p: Big dams and mining pollution are no longer the biggest threats to U.S. rivers, which are increasingly being polluted by more diverse activities, a conservation group said Wednesday.

Instead of being spoiled by major projects, which environmentalists have been able to turn back, waters are being damaged by forces that are harder to combat, including local development, feedlot operations, farms and communities.
"In short, what we see coming is death by a thousand cuts," Rebecca Wodder, president of American Rivers, said on issuing the group's annual ranking of the most endangered U.S. rivers.

The Missouri River moved to the top of the list this year because of all the engineering work that has changed the natural course of the river, draining life from the water to make way for barge traffic and to control floods.

By contrast, the Clarks Fork River, named the most imperiled river the previous three years, was dropped from the list completely because the White House worked out a deal to block a proposed mine outside Yellowstone National Park that threatened the river.
Major PCB (polychlorinated biphenyl) pollution made the upper Hudson River in New York the second most endangered river this year, the group said.

While the Environmental Protection Agency earlier had said the river, one of the worst toxic waste dumps in the country, should not be dredged to clean it up, American Rivers said the best way to solve the problem would be to dredge it.
The San Joaquin in California, the Washington D.C. region's Potomac and Mill Creek in Ohio were the three rivers facing the worst pollution from farming and developers.

American Rivers said the south branch of the Potomac, the source of much of the river's water supply, "is clogged with excrement from corporate poultry farms and cattle feedlots," threatening local drinking water supplies.
The third most endangered river was the White Salmon in Washington state, the only one among the 10 most imperiled where a hydropower dam was considered the biggest challenge.
Environmentalists are pressing for the Condit Dam, whose license has expired, to be removed. But federal regulators want the owner to install fish passages instead.

Other rivers facing the biggest threats are Pinto Creek in Arizona and Wolf River in Wisconsin because of mines; the lower Colorado River because of federal subsidies for water use; and the Tennessee River because of the proposed elimination of federal subsidies for environmental protection.
